title: Boundary of Binary Tree
statement:
Given a binary tree, print the nodes on its boundary in **anti-clockwise** order, starting from the root. The boundary is the concatenation of the following parts, and no node may appear twice:

- The **root**.
- The **left boundary**: start at the root's left child and walk down, moving to the left child when there is one and otherwise to the right child, until you would reach a leaf. Leaves are not part of the left boundary. If the root has no left child, the left boundary is empty.
- The **leaves**, from left to right. The root counts as a leaf only when it is the only node, in which case it is printed once.
- The **right boundary**: start at the root's right child and walk down, moving to the right child when there is one and otherwise to the left child, until you would reach a leaf. Leaves are not part of it. Print these nodes in **bottom-to-top** order. If the root has no right child, the right boundary is empty.

The tree may be completely unbalanced, and node values may repeat; nodes are distinguished by their position, not their value.

**Follow-up:** In the interview you may be asked to write the tree class yourself (for example in Java), to make the solution work for any shape of tree, and to produce the boundary with a single traversal.
input_format: A single line containing the tree in level order, values separated by spaces, with `null` for a missing child. A missing node has no children listed; trailing `null` values are omitted. The first value is the root and is never `null`.
output_format: Print the boundary values, separated by single spaces, on one line.

examples.explanation: The root is 1 and it has no left child, so the left boundary is empty. The leaves, left to right, are 3 and 4. The right boundary goes 1 -> 2 and stops before the leaf 4; reversed it is just 2. Result: `1 3 4 2`.

Root 1. Left boundary: 2 (its left child 4 is a leaf, so we stop). Leaves left to right: 4, 7, 8, 6. Right boundary: 3 (its right child 6 is a leaf). Result: `1 2 4 7 8 6 3`. Node 5 is neither on an edge nor a leaf, so it is skipped.
A single node is both the root and a leaf, and is printed once.

complexity.space: O(h) for recursion, where h is the tree height (O(n) in the worst case)

hints: Split the work into three independent pieces: the left edge, the leaves, and the right edge.
For the two edges, follow the child pointers as described, but stop before a leaf so that leaves are not printed twice. Collect the right edge and reverse it.
Leaves can be gathered with any traversal that visits the left subtree before the right. With a very deep (skewed) tree, prefer an explicit stack to recursion.
